blocks.text: Each week we highlight the noteworthy titles that have recently hit streaming platforms in the United States. Check out this week’s selections below and past round-ups here .

Martha Marcy May Marlene, Simon Kille r, and Christine producer Melody C. Roscher’s strong directorial debut Bird in Hand follows a bride-to-be returning to her rural hometown for wedding planning as unresolved tensions crop up. While the plot machinations can feel a bit obvious from the get-go, the performances are universally impressive (particularly from lead Alisha Wainwright), and Roscher proves to have a strong tonal handle on the material, weaving dexterously around complicated feelings of identity and family while injecting a sense of life and humanity in every scene. – Jordan R.
Everybody to Kenmure Street (Felipe Bustos Sierra)

As ICE wreaks havoc in communities across America, it would be advantageous to look at the activist tactics on display in Felipe Bustos Sierra’s gripping Sundance documentary Everybody to Kenmure Street , which provides a detailed look at the way a Scottish community fought back within seconds when their neighbors were rounded up for deportation back in 2021. – Jordan R.

“Look into my eyes / can you see they’re open wide / would I lie to you?” Those lyrics linger in the air as a soft whisper for only a moment before the accompanying piano notes carry them away and into the beginning of Gentle Monster , the latest from Corsage director Marie Kreutzer. One might already suspect that the cover of such an emblematic ’90s pop song, pulsating under the fingertips of the film’s protagonist, Lucy (Léa Seydoux), could serve as exposition in some way. Yet the growl camouflaged in Seydoux’s silky voice might just as well be a sign of fatigue—the Lucy we meet in this opening scene is still adapting to quiet, countryside life from a career of touring European capitals. When her husband Philip (Laurence Rupp) interrupts her practice by rushing in, full-on panic attack, it’s the patience in her consoling voice that signals it’s not the first time she has stopped mid-song to make room for him. – Savina P. ( full review )

For as wild and uncomfortable as Obsession becomes, it is less a question of where the film is going than how it’s going to get there and what path it will take. To Barker’s credit, however, it never feels like he’s stalling for time; a lot of the film is spent observing Bear and his other co-workers, including Sarah (Megan Lawless), the owner’s daughter, who perhaps has a bit of a crush on Bear. Both she and Ian find Nikki’s sudden change a bit odd, concerned that Bear may be taking advantage of a mental breakdown. It’s a development that shows Barker has something on his mind, perhaps recognizing that another version of this movie could be horrific in its misogyny. – Devan S. ( full review )

After a clunky opening setting the table for his time-hopping reworking of Homer’s epic, Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey settles into a rhythm of melding awe-worthy spectacle with the emotional toll of a seemingly never-ending journey of despair and sacrifice. What I was most struck by, even for all its fantastical elements, is how much Nolan mines from the rather spare natural settings to instill a grounded sense of vastness when it comes to Odysseus’ journey. While one wishes for a bit more patience to take it all in, the trademark propulsiveness of the director works wonders as we discover the ingenuity of each setpiece. For another perspective, read Nick Newman’s eloquent review , which details why the technical feat of shooting entirely in IMAX has its drawbacks. – Jordan R.

Working with her sister Anna—a 38-year-old Korean adoptee with a developmental disability—director Liz Sargent’s sensitive drama Take Me Home is both witty and heartbreaking. It serves as an indictment of a system that would force a father to abandon his adopted daughter just to secure the care they both need, all while ending on an optimistic note. For much of the film, Sargent’s picture exists in a mode of social realism before an abrupt ending that isn’t just a tonal shift, but feels intentionally like a different movie that also happens to star Anna. – John F. ( full review )

Old ladies need movies as festivals like TIFF need world premieres. So is the case with A Talent for Murder , which can be applied to a subgenre known as Mirrenslop. Other highlights (or rather lowlights) include the Israeli hagiography Golda and, like that film, this may get a distributor its one token Oscar nomination in the makeup category. As such, Mirren is done up to play one of America’s greatest writers, Patricia Highsmith. Best known for The Talented Mr. Ripley , an undeniable masterpiece, the author used crime fiction to explore what feels like all of human experience. Would she approve of this heavily fictionalized account of her last year on earth? Likely not. – Ethan V. ( full review )

To the public, Anthony Bourdain was a carefully constructed persona: the fine-dining chef who waxed poetic about the joys of “regular” food and traveled to far-flung locales that made him want to throttle Henry Kissinger on shows like Parts Unknown . He would be the first to admit he wasn’t perfect, cataloging his faults in bestsellers like Kitchen Confidential and Medium Raw while sharing his thoughts on various blogs and social platforms up until his tragic suicide in 2018. With such presence, it would seem like his life was plenty covered; Kitchen Confidential even had a Fox sitcom in 2005 starring a young Bradley Cooper. Matt Johnson’s Tony recognizes this tall order and, like many of the better biopics, chooses to focus on a small, pivotal section of Bourdain’s story: the first couple chapters of Kitchen Confidential. – Devan S. ( full review )

Spending nearly four decades in prison for a murder they did not commit, Andrew Stewart, Ransom Watkins, and Alfred Chestnut work through the psychological toll of wrongful imprisonment in Dawn Porter’s powerful documentary When a Witness Recants . Backed by Ta-Nehisi Coates, who is featured making a personal connection to the story, it’s a maddening, thorough look at the failures of the American justice system, with an unforgettable finale. – Jordan R.
